subject: history
title: Racial Policy and Kristallnacht
welcome_lead: From the boycott of April 1933 to the November 1938 pogrom.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on Nazi anti-Jewish policy, Nuremberg Laws and Kristallnacht.
final_note: You have charted the cumulative radicalisation of persecution.

concepts.def: One-day SA-led boycott of Jewish shops on 1 April 1933, ineffective but signalling state-sponsored persecution.
Law of 7 April 1933 dismissing Jews and political opponents from public employment.
Passed on 15 September 1935 stripping Jews of citizenship and prohibiting intermarriage.
Forced transfer of Jewish-owned businesses and property to non-Jewish Germans, accelerating after 1937.
Pogrom on 9-10 November 1938 destroying 267 synagogues, killing about 91 Jews and arresting 30,000 men.
'National community' idealised as racially pure, excluding Jews, Roma and others deemed undesirable.

walkthroughs.body_html: From April 1933 the regime issued laws restricting Jews from civil service, professions and universities. The Reich Citizenship Law and Law for the Protection of German Blood (Nuremberg Laws, 15 September 1935) defined Jewishness by descent and banned intermarriage. Around 400 anti-Jewish decrees followed by 1939. Aryanisation accelerated under Goring's Four Year Plan from 1936.

The 17 August 1938 decree required Jews to add 'Israel' or 'Sara' to their names. On 7 November Herschel Grynszpan assassinated diplomat vom Rath in Paris. Goebbels used the funeral on 9 November to orchestrate a 'spontaneous' pogrom. SA and Hitler Youth burned 267 synagogues, killed about 91 Jews and arrested 30,000 men. A 1 billion Reichsmark fine was imposed on Jewish communities.

Intentionalists like Lucy Dawidowicz argued Hitler always intended Jewish destruction. Functionalists such as Hans Mommsen and Christopher Browning saw cumulative radicalisation as competing agencies (SD, Gauleiters, Four Year Plan office) escalated measures. Kristallnacht marked transition from emigration policy to violent expropriation, prefiguring the wartime path to genocide after 1941.
